e.etymology: From Swahili malaika, 'angel', borrowed from Arabic mala'ika, 'angels'. The Swahili love song Malaika, recorded by Miriam Makeba and many others, carried the word around the world.

assoc.t: Malaika, Swahili love song sung by Miriam Makeba

e.etymology: A respelling of Jackson, an English surname meaning 'son of Jack'. Jack began as a medieval pet form of John.

An elaboration of Eliana with an -i ending, in the style of Caribbean Spanish names such as Eliany and Elianny. Eliana is read as Hebrew for 'my God has answered' and also descends from the Roman name Aeliana.
The Latinate form of French Henriette, the feminine of Henri (Henry), from Germanic heim, 'home', and ric, 'ruler'. Harriet began as its everyday spoken form in England.
namesakes: Henrietta Lacks (source of the HeLa cell line)

assoc.t: Henrietta Lacks, source of the HeLa cell line

e.etymology: A 20th-century American coinage from Kay and the -lyn ending, one of a large family of spellings that includes Kaylin and Kaelyn.
From Sanskrit aditya, 'belonging to Aditi'. The Adityas are the sons of the goddess Aditi in the Vedas, and the word became a name of the sun god Surya.
A Spanish contraction of Magdalena or of María Elena, also used in Scandinavia as a form of Magdalena. Malena is the title of a classic Argentine tango.

assoc.t: Malèna, Monica Bellucci's title role in the 2000 film

e.etymology: From Arabic ghayth, 'rain', especially plentiful rain that brings relief after drought, so the name also carries the sense of help and deliverance.
e.note: The Arabic gh sound has no English match, so most Americans will say GAYTH with a hard g.

e.etymology: From Merlinus, the medieval Latin form of Welsh Myrddin, from Celtic words for 'sea' and 'stronghold'. Geoffrey of Monmouth gave the name to the wizard of the King Arthur legends.
namesakes: Merlin (wizard of the King Arthur legends)
Merlin Olsen (Hall of Fame football player and actor)

assoc.t: Merlin, wizard and adviser to King Arthur
merlin, a small falcon
Merlin Bird ID, Cornell's bird identification app

e.etymology: An anglicized spelling of Arabic Khalil, 'close friend'. The Lebanese-American poet Kahlil Gibran, author of The Prophet, kept this spelling after a Boston school registered him under it.
namesakes: Kahlil Gibran (poet, author of The Prophet)

assoc.t: Kahlil Gibran, author of The Prophet

e.etymology: From the surname of actress Jennifer Aniston, whose Greek-born father's family took it in place of Anastassakis. That name comes from Anastasios, from the Greek word for resurrection.

assoc.t: Jennifer Aniston, Friends actress
Anniston, Alabama (spelled with two n's)

e.etymology: A Czech and South Slavic pet form of Ivana, the feminine of Ivan, the Slavic form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'.
namesakes: Ivanka Trump (businesswoman, daughter of Donald Trump)

assoc.t: Ivanka Trump, daughter of President Donald Trump

e.etymology: A streamlined spelling of Rowan or Roan. Rowan comes from the Irish surname Ó Ruadháin, 'descendant of the little red-haired one', and is also the name of the rowan tree.
A recent American coinage that puts a Z on the -axton ending of Paxton, Jaxton and Braxton.
A respelling of Destiny, the English word used as a name since the 1970s. The word comes from Old French destinée, which this spelling echoes.
From Nigellus, the medieval Latin form of Neil (Irish Niall), shaped by Latin niger, 'black'. Revived by 19th-century writers such as Walter Scott, it became a signature British name.
namesakes: Nigel Thornberry (father in The Wild Thornberrys)
Nigel Farage (British politician)
Nigel Lythgoe (TV dance-show judge and producer)
e.note: Americans tend to hear Nigel as the stereotypical British name.

e.etymology: A name with several sources: the Armenian hero-king Ara the Beautiful, a Korean girl's name, and Latin ara, 'altar', which names a southern constellation.
namesakes: Ara Parseghian (Notre Dame football coach)

assoc.t: Ara, the Altar, a southern constellation

e.etymology: Best known from Princess Merida of Pixar's Brave (2012). Mérida is also a city in Spain, with namesakes in Mexico and Venezuela; its name comes from Latin Emerita, a colony founded for retired soldiers.
namesakes: Merida (archer princess of Pixar's Brave)

assoc.t: Princess Merida, archer heroine of Pixar's Brave
Mérida, capital of Yucatán, Mexico

e.etymology: A recent American coinage in the pattern of Amari, Anaya and Imani.
e.note: In Hindi and Urdu, anari is an everyday word for a clumsy or unskilled person.

e.etymology: The English spelling of French Émile, from the Roman family name Aemilius, traditionally linked to Latin aemulus, 'rival'. Rousseau's 1762 treatise on education is titled Émile.
namesakes: Émile Zola (French novelist)
Emile Hirsch (actor)

assoc.t: Emile, Remy's brother in Pixar's Ratatouille

e.meaning: of Olympus, home of the gods
e.etymology: From Greek Olympia, from Olympos, the mountain home of the gods. Olympia was also the sanctuary of Zeus where the ancient Olympic Games were held.
namesakes: Olympia Dukakis (Oscar-winning actress)
Olympia Snowe (US senator from Maine)

assoc.t: Olympia, capital of Washington State
Olympia, Greek site of the ancient Olympic Games
Mr. Olympia bodybuilding contest

e.etymology: From an English surname and place name made of Old English brycg, 'bridge', and ham, 'homestead'. Its use as a first name honors the Mormon pioneer leader Brigham Young.
namesakes: Brigham Young (Latter-day Saint leader who founded Salt Lake City)

assoc.t: Brigham Young, Mormon pioneer leader
the Brigham, Boston's Brigham and Women's Hospital

e.note: Strongly tied to the Latter-day Saint (Mormon) faith through Brigham Young.

e.meaning: prosperous spear, a Scottish form of Edgar
e.etymology: A Scottish surname and first name, generally taken as a Galloway form of Edgar, from Old English ead, 'prosperity', and gar, 'spear'.
A spelling of Yusuf, the Arabic and Persian form of Joseph, from Hebrew Yosef, 'he will add'. Yusuf is a prophet in the Quran, the Joseph of Genesis.
namesakes: Yusef Lateef (jazz saxophonist)
Yusef Salaam (Exonerated Five member, New York City councilman)

e.etymology: An Italian name cut down from Germanic names built on land, 'land, territory', and a short form of Orlando and Rolando. Star Wars and Formula 1 driver Lando Norris brought it to American parents.
namesakes: Lando Calrissian (Star Wars character)
Lando Norris (Formula 1 driver)

assoc.t: Lando Calrissian, Star Wars smuggler turned general
Lando Norris, British Formula 1 driver

e.etymology: A modern American spelling close to Alaia, a Basque name meaning joyful, and to Alayah and Aaliyah.
From Sanskrit krishna, 'dark, black, dark blue'. Krishna is one of the most widely worshipped Hindu deities, the eighth avatar of Vishnu and the teacher of the Bhagavad Gita.

assoc.t: Krishna, Hindu god and eighth avatar of Vishnu
Hare Krishna movement and its chant

e.etymology: A respelling of Chase, an English surname that began as a nickname for a huntsman, from Old French chacier, 'to hunt'.
namesakes: Chayce Beckham (American Idol winner and country singer)

e.meaning: garden, orchard; also Latin for song
e.etymology: A respelling of Carmen, the Spanish name taken from Our Lady of Mount Carmel. Carmel is Hebrew for 'garden, orchard', and the name was reshaped by Latin carmen, 'song'.
The name of the Goblin King played by David Bowie in the 1986 film Labyrinth, which brought it into use. It reads as a blend of Jared and Gareth.
namesakes: Jareth (Goblin King played by David Bowie in Labyrinth)

assoc.t: Jareth the Goblin King, David Bowie's role in Labyrinth

e.etymology: A respelling of Haven, the English word for a safe harbor or refuge, from Old English hæfen, 'port'.
The Greek and Latin form of Ezra, from Hebrew ezra, 'help'. It is the form used in Spanish, Portuguese and French Bibles and in the books of Esdras in the Apocrypha.
